sections.h2: Baton Rouge: city and parish run together
sections.html:
The Louisiana capital shares one consolidated government with East Baton Rouge Parish. Sellers inside the city limits therefore deal with parish offices for permits, blight enforcement and recording.

The city counted 227,470 residents in 2020 across 86.32 square miles of land, and Greater Baton Rouge held 870,569 people that year. That makes the buyer pool much larger than the city itself. Interstates 10, 12 and 110 connect neighborhoods such as Highland Road, the Garden District, Goodwood, Scotlandville, Mid-City and the Perkins Road area, and Baton Rouge Metropolitan Airport serves the region.

State offices, LSU, Southern University and the river port keep demand steady. Roofs, drainage and air conditioning age fast in a climate that averages 61.94 inches of rain a year, and buyers price that wear into their offers.

Under half of occupied homes in the city are lived in by their owners. These 2020 to 2024 numbers describe the city as a whole, so they say little about any one street. Ask a local agent or appraiser for comparable sales close to your address before you decide what price to hope for.

With over half of homes rented, plenty of local sellers are landlords. A tenant in place, a lease running beyond closing or a unit emptied by a rough move-out changes the options compared with selling your own residence.

sections.h2: How did the August 2016 flood change selling in Baton Rouge?
sections.html:
The August 2016 flood still comes up in nearly every conversation with buyers and lenders. Twenty to 30 inches of rain fell over several days, and rescues topped 30,000, while over 50,000 homes across southern Louisiana were damaged or destroyed. Roughly 109,000 Louisiana homes took water, 79,000 of them in East Baton Rouge and Livingston Parishes. Residential damage was estimated at $3.8 billion, with $2.3 billion of it in those two parishes.

Expect questions like these if your house took water:

  • Did the house flood in 2016, and what repairs were permitted?
  • Is there a flood zone determination or elevation record on file?
  • Can you show invoices for post-2016 work?

A buyer who pulls permit history may find unpermitted repairs from that period, and flood zone details can change whether a lender will close. For 2026 the state commission publishes a mandatory Property Disclosure form, so read it early and answer water history questions carefully.

The Comite River Diversion, a 12-mile channel built to cut headwater flooding, is not finished. All 23 contracts had been awarded by the close of fiscal year 2025, and six are under construction. Do not count on lower risk for a given street yet.

Weeds and brush that reach eight inches count as a nuisance under the city-parish code. A property with a blight violation gets a notice giving the owner 15 days to fix it, plus a blight court date.

Should the problem remain by the hearing, the court may enter a judgment for a fine and costs. The Department of Development may then clear the property and place a lien for the cost. Such a lien sticks to the land, so it gets paid at closing.

  • Report a problem property at 311.
  • Questions about a notice go to Neighborhood Improvement at 225-389-8680.
  • The Department of Development handles construction permits and code enforcement for the parish at 225-389-3171.

Heirs and owners of empty houses often find a blight case only when a lien appears in the title search, so call before you list. The city also has a page on adjudicated property, useful if an inherited house has a history of unpaid taxes.

sections.h2: How a sale closes in East Baton Rouge Parish
sections.html:
Under the Civil Code, selling real estate or promising to sell it takes an authentic act or an act under private signature. The authentic version is signed with a notary and two witnesses, which explains why closings here run through a notary.

After signing, the act of sale is filed with the Clerk of Court for East Baton Rouge Parish. Its Recording Department indexes conveyances by vendee and vendor and collects fees at filing. The number is (225) 389-3985, and the mailing address is P.O. Box 1991, Baton Rouge, LA 70821-1991.

New mandatory forms for 2026, among them the Property Disclosure and the Residential Agreement to Buy or Sell, became effective January 1, 2026. Your closing professional can tell you which ones your sale needs.

sections.h2: Ways to sell a Baton Rouge house
sections.html:
Three routes are common: list the house, sell it yourself, or accept a cash offer from an investor. Condition, flood history and your timeline decide which one fits.

  • Listing with an agent: Fits a clean, repaired house if you can sit through showings, financing and an appraisal.
  • For sale by owner: Disclosures, buyer screening and notary scheduling become your job.
  • Cash sale as-is: Makes sense for flood damage, postponed repairs, a tenant or a blight notice, since no lender's inspection stands in the way.

Whoever you sell to, read every page of the contract, including any cancellation language, before you sign.

sections.h2: Checklist before you accept an offer
sections.html:
Look at the address first: flood history, code cases, permits and liens. Any of them can move the price or stop a lender.

  • Pull your flood zone and any 2016 water history.
  • Ask 311 or Neighborhood Improvement whether a blight case is open.
  • Order a title search of the conveyance and mortgage records.
  • If you inherited the house, settle who may sign.
  • Keep copies of repair invoices and permits from post-2016 work.

An hour on these steps often saves weeks. Landlords should also dig out the lease and note its end date, because a tenant affects showings and the date keys can change hands.

sections.h2: What to expect on closing day
sections.html: Closing is a signing appointment at a notary or title office. Bring a photo ID. The notary has the act of sale, payoff figures and settlement statement ready. Taxes, a mortgage balance and recording fees are taken from your proceeds, and the signed act then goes to the clerk. Request the statement early so you can question any fee.

faqs.q: Do I need a notary to sell a house in Baton Rouge?
faqs.a: Almost always. Louisiana sales of real estate are made by authentic act or act under private signature, and in practice you sign with a notary. A title company or closing attorney normally sets this up.

faqs.q: Does a Baton Rouge house that flooded in 2016 have to be disclosed?
faqs.a: Buyers and insurers will probably ask, and a mandatory 2026 Property Disclosure form exists. Check with your closing professional how it applies, answer plainly and save repair records.

faqs.q: What happens if my Baton Rouge house has a blight violation?
faqs.a: The owner gets a notice with 15 days to correct the problem and a blight court date. If it is not cleared, the court can assess a fine and costs, and the city can clear the property and place a lien. Call 311 or 225-389-8680 to ask about status.

faqs.q: Where are Baton Rouge deeds recorded?
faqs.a: The Recording Department of the parish Clerk of Court handles it, at (225) 389-3985. You pay fees when the document is filed.

faqs.q: How many Baton Rouge homes are owner-occupied?
faqs.a: Roughly 47.8 percent for 2020 to 2024, and the median owner-occupied home is valued at $234,700. Both are citywide numbers, so a specific house may differ.
